sentences.text: They did it every evening after supper.
They made it a small ritual.
Harabeoji would take one sheet from the box, and he would think about that week — which he did not always remember specifically, but he remembered enough — and he would write something.
Sometimes it was a fact about the weather.
Sometimes it was a memory of Halmoni.
Sometimes it was what he had eaten.
Once he wrote, at the bottom of a sheet, in his very quiet hand: This week I did not remember to eat lunch three days in a row.
It is embarrassing to write this down but true.
Ji-eun read it.
She looked up at him.
He smiled a little, without any lightness, and shrugged.
Ji-eun also wrote, on some sheets.
She would ask him, what was Halmoni like that week?
And he would say something, and she would write it in her own handwriting — which was much rounder and more childish than his — on the sheet.
She wrote things like: Halmoni sang while she washed the rice.
She wrote: Halmoni put a little butter on Ji-eun's hand when Ji-eun pinched her mother.

That story Harabeoji told her one evening — that Halmoni believed a small kindness stopped a small unkindness, so she always answered a pinch with butter — made Ji-eun laugh out loud for the first time since she had arrived.
They did not finish.
There were fifty-eight sheets in the box, and they got through thirty-one over the two weeks Ji-eun was there.
Some evenings they only did one.
Some evenings they did four.
Some evenings Harabeoji did not want to.
He would say, "Not tonight, Ji-eun.
Tonight we watch the persimmon." And they would sit on the porch and watch the persimmon tree not do anything in particular, and that was fine.
Sometimes, during the day, while Harabeoji was working at the vat and Ji-eun was watching, she would think about the sheets in the box.
She thought about how a week could go by, and not be counted, and still be there.

She thought about her mother, and the baby coming in September, and how her mother had said, when Ji-eun had asked how you counted time with a new baby, that you didn't — you just tried to notice as much as you could, and if you noticed enough, the time didn't need counting.
Ji-eun had not really understood that when her mother had said it.
She thought maybe she was beginning to.
On the last evening of Ji-eun's visit, they put the thirty-one dated sheets back into the wooden box, carefully, in the order they had been made.
The remaining twenty-seven — the ones they had not yet gotten to — Harabeoji put in a smaller neat stack beside the box.
He said, "When you come next summer, we do more.
Perhaps we finish.
Perhaps not.
Now they are two boxes — the ones we have marked and the ones still to mark.
That is fine.
That is progress."
He carried the box back across the courtyard to the workshop and put it back on the low shelf in the corner.
But he did not push it all the way back into the shadow.
He set it a little forward, so that when he came into the workshop each morning, he would see it.
Ji-eun watched him do this and did not say anything.
He came back to the house.
He said, "You have done a good thing here, Ji-eun.
I did not know I needed to do that.
I thought I had finished with those sheets.
It turned out I had not."
In the morning, before she left for the train, he gave her something.
It was a single sheet of hanji, rolled into a small loose tube and tied with cotton string.
He said, "This is one of the unnumbered sheets.
I have marked it for you.
It is yours to keep." Ji-eun untied it and looked.
In Harabeoji's careful small hand, along the bottom of the sheet, he had written: The week Ji-eun was eleven and came to see her Harabeoji alone for the first time and found the box.
This is one of ours.
Ji-eun rolled it up again carefully.
She said, "But Harabeoji, this was not from that year.
This is now." He said, "Yes.
But it is the same box.
It belongs there.
The counting has changed again.
Now every summer you come, we mark one sheet.
Not by number.
By what happened.

In fifty years, when I am long gone, there will be a box in some corner somewhere with these sheets in it, and someone — maybe your child, maybe your grandchild — will find it, and they will know that a girl came to Andong every summer to see her grandfather, and that they marked a sheet together each time, and that was one way of counting."
He walked her to the station.
They did not talk very much on the way.
That was normal.
At the platform he waited with her, and when the train pulled in he gave her a small quiet hug — Harabeoji did not hug easily, but this time he did — and helped her step up into the carriage.
He said, "Give my love to your mother.
Take care of the baby, when it comes.
Come back in the winter if you can." She said she would try.
The train pulled away.
Ji-eun sat by the window with the rolled hanji sheet in her lap.
She watched the small city and then the rice paddies and then the mountains go past.
She thought about the box in the corner of the workshop, with the thirty-one marked sheets and the twenty-seven still to be marked, and now the one that had joined them.
She thought about the years, all the years, that were still to come.
She thought about her grandfather, alone in the hanok, walking back across the courtyard to the workshop right now, probably.
Not to work.
Just to sit for a moment.
To look at the box.
To be with it.
She hoped the persimmon tree was doing something small and quiet outside his door.
